title: Schengen Visa Rejections Cost Indian Travellers Rs 154 Crore Despite Record Applications
excerpt: Over 1.81 lakh Indian applications were denied in 2025, with a 15.8 percent rejection rate and non-refundable fees of €90 per application driving the staggering financial toll.
body:
• More than 181,000 Schengen visa applications from India were rejected in 2025, costing applicants an estimated Rs 154 crore (€16 million) in non-refundable fees
  • Slovenia had the highest rejection rate for Indian applicants at 46.1 percent, followed by Bulgaria at 37 percent and Greece at 33 percent, while Germany maintained a relatively low 10.5 percent rate despite processing over 153,000 applications
  • Insufficient or inconsistent financial proof was the leading cause of rejections, accounting for more than 30 percent of refusals in a review of 12,000 Indian cases

Indian travellers lost an estimated Rs 154 crore in non-refundable visa fees after more than 181,000 Schengen visa applications were rejected in 2025, according to data released by the European Commission. The figure represents one of the largest financial hits from visa denials for any nationality globally.

Out of more than 11.5 lakh applications filed by Indians last year — a record — roughly one in every six was denied. The 15.8 percent rejection rate came even as outbound travel from India continued to surge past pre-pandemic levels, with total departures reaching 3.08 crore in 2025.

Where Rejections Hit Hardest

The rejection landscape varied sharply by destination. Slovenia emerged as the most challenging Schengen country for Indian applicants, turning down nearly half of all applications with a non-issuance rate of 46.1 percent. Bulgaria followed at 37 percent, and Greece — despite being among the most popular European destinations for Indian tourists — rejected roughly one in three applications.

France topped the absolute numbers, denying over 31,000 Indian applications, followed by Switzerland and Germany. Belgium and Denmark, by contrast, reported some of the lowest rejection rates at 7.7 and 6.9 percent respectively.

Germany presented a notable outlier: despite handling over 153,000 Indian applications, one of the highest volumes in Europe, it maintained a rejection rate of around 10.5 percent — suggesting that high volume alone does not drive high refusal rates.

Why Applications Fail

A review of more than 12,000 Indian cases from the 2024-25 fiscal year, conducted by visa analytics platform VisaVerge, found that insufficient or inconsistent financial proof was the single biggest trigger, accounting for more than 30 percent of refusals.

The problem was not limited to low-income applicants. Bank statements that did not align with declared income, itineraries that did not match hotel bookings, and travel insurance that failed to meet the mandatory €30,000 medical coverage threshold all contributed to denials.

Other common triggers included weak evidence of ties to India, vague travel purpose, missing old passports, employment letters that lacked explicit leave approvals, and applications submitted to the wrong consulate — a procedural error that catches travellers off guard under Schengen rules requiring submission to the embassy of the primary destination country.

The True Cost

The Rs 154 crore headline figure accounts only for the standard €90 application fee, recently hiked from €80. When factoring in visa facilitation centre service charges, the rupee equivalent rises further depending on the exchange rate at the time of application.

Travel industry experts say the actual economic damage is significantly higher. Pre-booked, non-refundable flights, hotel reservations, travel insurance premiums and time spent gathering documentation all compound the loss. For applicants who booked travel before receiving their visa decision — a common practice given lengthy processing times — a rejection can mean thousands of rupees in additional sunk costs.

"The true economic toll is significantly higher when factoring in secondary losses from pre-booked, non-refundable hotels, flight cancellations, and travel insurance premiums."

— Travel industry analysis, The Sunday Guardian

What Applicants Can Do

Visa consultants and travel experts recommend several strategies to improve approval odds. Applying through consulates with historically lower rejection rates, such as Belgium or Denmark, when the travel itinerary permits, can make a difference. Ensuring bank statements show consistent savings rather than sudden large deposits, providing clear and detailed travel itineraries, and submitting documents well in advance of peak travel season are also cited as best practices.

For the Indian diaspora, the numbers underscore a persistent friction in global mobility. Despite India's growing economic clout and travel spending, its citizens continue to face some of the steepest bureaucratic barriers to entering Europe — a gap between aspiration and access that shows little sign of narrowing.
